prompt.context: Our client sells scooters and motorcycles in an emerging-market country. Recently, revenue and profits have been declining. Customers are typically lower-income consumers who cannot afford a car. Customers use the scooters to get to work and get around for everyday tasks.
prompt.question: What might be causing the dip in revenue? What can the client do to reverse this trend?

clarifying_info.q: What markets does the client operate in?
clarifying_info.a: An emerging-market country; the client sells both scooters and motorcycles.

clarifying_info.q: Has the client's market share changed?
clarifying_info.a: No, market share has remained constant at 70% for scooters and 10% for motorcycles.
Scooter price is unchanged at $500. Motorcycle price dropped from $600 to $500 over the past 5 years.

clarifying_info.q: Has the overall market grown or shrunk?
clarifying_info.a: The scooter market declined from 1,000,000 to 900,000 units. The motorcycle market grew from 100,000 to 500,000 units.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client want to pursue the motorcycle segment?
clarifying_info.a: The company has not pursued any expansion in the motorcycle category and would prefer to improve on the scooter side.

exhibits.title: Scooter and Motorcycle Data – 5 Years Ago vs. Today (Interviewer Copy)
exhibits.shows: A two-section data table comparing company and customer metrics for scooters and motorcycles across two time periods (5 years ago and today).

exhibits.title: Scooter and Motorcycle Data – Candidate Copy
exhibits.shows: Candidate-facing version of the same two-section data table (scooter and motorcycle metrics, 5 years ago vs. today).

data.note: Same figures as Exhibit 1 — this is the sheet given directly to the candidate.

framework: Revenue decomposition: Revenue = Market size x Market share x Price. Identify which driver(s) changed for each product.
Cost structure: Profit per unit = Price - Fixed cost - Variable cost. Verify margins are unchanged or identify cost creep.
Customer value analysis: Calculate total cost of ownership (TCO) per year for scooter vs. motorcycle to understand whether substitute competition is driving scooter demand down.
Growth levers: Evaluate options to reverse the revenue decline — market development, product improvement, pricing, or share gain.
Market expansion: Consider whether entering adjacent markets or geographies can offset the shrinking scooter segment.

questions.prompt: Calculate the revenue decline on the scooter side over the past 5 years.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute revenue = units sold x price for both periods and quantify the gap.

math.setup: Units sold = Market size x Market share. Revenue = Units x Price.
steps: Revenue decline = $350M - $315M = $35M (a 10% drop driven entirely by market shrinkage, not share or price)
math.answer: Scooter revenue fell by $35M (10%), entirely due to the market shrinking 10% from 1M to 900K units. Market share and price are unchanged.

questions.prompt: Calculate the revenue on the motorcycle side over the same period and assess the net company-level picture.
questions.guidance: Market grew 5x but price fell and share is low. Candidate should compute both periods and note the partial offset.

math.setup: Same formula: Units = Market size x Market share; Revenue = Units x Price.
steps: Motorcycle revenue increased by $19M despite price drop, because volume surged 5x.
Net company revenue change: -$35M (scooter) + $19M (motorcycle) = -$16M overall decline
math.answer: Motorcycle revenue rose by $19M, but does not fully offset the $35M scooter decline, leaving the company down ~$16M overall.

questions.prompt: Calculate and compare the annual cost of ownership for a scooter vs. a motorcycle to understand whether customers are switching.
questions.guidance: TCO per year should include amortized purchase price (net of salvage), plus annual maintenance. Gas cost depends on assumptions about gas price and annual mileage — candidate should flag this dependency and work through the math. The key insight is that motorcycles are slightly cheaper or roughly equivalent to own, making them an attractive substitute for price-sensitive consumers.

math.setup: Annual ownership cost = (Purchase price - Salvage value) / Useful life + Annual maintenance. Gas cost = (Annual miles / MPG) x Gas price per gallon — candidate must assume or ask for gas price and annual miles.
steps: Gas cost is identical for both (same MPG = 60), so gas does not differentiate them — it adds equally to both.
Net result: Motorcycle is ~$12.50/yr cheaper to own than a scooter at current prices.
math.answer: A motorcycle costs approximately $12.50/yr less than a scooter at current prices (excluding gas, which is equal). For price-sensitive consumers, this tips preference toward motorcycles and helps explain the market shift.

questions.prompt: What are the root causes of the revenue and profit decline?
questions.guidance: Candidate should synthesize the data into clear causal drivers: (1) the scooter market is shrinking — likely because the motorcycle market grew 5x, offering a slightly cheaper TCO; (2) the company did not capture the growing motorcycle segment (10% share vs. 70% in scooters); (3) motorcycle price dropped from $600 to $500, compressing what could have been higher motorcycle margins.

questions.prompt: What can the client do to reverse the trend? (The client prefers to focus on the scooter side and grow the market.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should generate a range of ideas, grouped by lever. Strong candidates will address both demand-side (make scooters more attractive to current non-buyers) and supply-side/cost levers. Ideas should be grounded in the customer profile (low-income, utility-focused).

brainstorming.prompt: The client wants to grow the scooter market and reverse the revenue decline. What ideas would you propose?

categories.name: Reduce cost of ownership to compete with motorcycles
ideas: Engineer higher gas mileage (e.g., 80 mpg) to lower fuel costs for customers
Lower the retail price through cost reduction or subsidized financing
Improve reliability / reduce maintenance costs through better engineering or warranty programs
Offer a trade-in or buy-back program to establish residual value (currently $0 salvage)

categories.name: Expand the addressable market
ideas: Target rural consumers who currently rely on walking or public transit
Offer microfinance or installment payment plans to reach consumers who cannot pay $500 upfront
Introduce a lower-priced entry model to attract first-time buyers
Partner with employers or governments to subsidize scooters for commuting workers

categories.name: Grow share within the existing scooter market
ideas: Increase dealer network / distribution in underserved areas
Invest in brand and after-sales service to differentiate from smaller competitors
Bundle maintenance packages to lower perceived TCO

categories.name: Explore adjacent growth
ideas: Enter new geographic markets in the same region
Consider light commercial variants (cargo scooters) to reach small business owners
Evaluate whether to aggressively grow the motorcycle segment given its 5x market expansion

recommendation: The revenue decline is primarily driven by the scooter market shrinking by 100,000 units, partly because motorcycles now offer a slightly lower total cost of ownership at parity pricing. The company did not participate in the motorcycle market's 5x growth.

To reverse the trend, the client should focus on reducing the total cost of ownership of the scooter — specifically engineering for higher fuel efficiency, improving reliability, and introducing installment financing — to make scooters more attractive than motorcycles for its target customer. Simultaneously, the client should pursue market development by expanding distribution and financing access to lower-income consumers currently priced out of the market.
risks: If motorcycle prices continue to fall or quality improves further, scooters may face sustained structural headwinds regardless of TCO improvements.
Lowering the retail price or adding financing compresses margins in the short term; the client must ensure unit economics remain positive.
Market development in new geographies or segments takes time and may require upfront investment in distribution infrastructure.
next_steps: Conduct detailed engineering analysis to identify the cost of achieving 80+ mpg and the resulting impact on customer TCO.
Pilot a micro-financing / installment program in one region and measure incremental unit volume.
Quantify the cost and feasibility of establishing a residual/buy-back value for scooters to narrow the TCO gap further.
Assess whether a selective entry into higher-growth motorcycle sub-segments would be value-accretive given the 10% share baseline.
